Models generally perform worse on the issues experts consider most important. Six of seven models score lowest on High-priority rubrics and highest on Low-priority rubrics; Grok 4.7 is the only exception, with nearly identical High and Medium performance. The gap is substantial for several models: DeepSeek V4 Pro rises from 45.4% on High-priority items to 75.3% on Low-priority items, while GPT-6 Astra rises from 42.8% to 67.3%. Much of this pattern also reflects the mix of actions rather than priority itself: 73% of Low-priority items are Preserve, the easiest action, against 11% of High-priority items.

Context-sensitive judgment remains harder than standard playbook execution.

The evaluation-dimension results largely reinforce the patterns above. Negotiation Restraint is the strongest dimension for every model, while Astra's 70.9% score on Escalation Judgment reflects its broad coverage of required escalations. Issue Prioritization also tracks the earlier weakness on High-priority issues: Grok leads at 62.7%, while Astra scores 31.1%.

The gap between Standard Position Execution and Situational Judgment points to a specific weakness: reconciling playbook rules with deal context. Standard Position Execution tests whether models follow unconditional playbook rules that apply regardless of deal facts. Situational Judgment tests the conditional rules, those that apply only when particular deal facts are present, and so requires models to reconcile the facts and commercial circumstances of the transaction with the playbook before deciding which rule governs. Every model scores 9 to 15 points lower on the latter. Grok, for example, falls from 62.6% on Standard Position Execution to 47.7% on Situational Judgment, while Gemini drops from 54.2% to 40.3%. The consistent gap underscores the difficulty of translating enterprise playbooks into context-sensitive negotiation decisions.

No-playbook scenarios place the greatest demands on contextual judgment. Models must determine appropriate negotiation positions from the commercial facts alone, without explicit company rules. Six of seven models score lowest in these scenarios. Most models score highest with single-agreement playbooks, while even multi-contract playbooks outperform no playbook despite their additional rule-selection complexity. These results reinforce the Situational Judgment findings: models struggle with context-sensitive decisions, but playbooks help orient their judgment in complex negotiations.

GPT-6 Astra is the exception. Its score rises from 43% on multi-contract playbooks to 46% on single-agreement playbooks and 50% with no playbook. That reversal does not line up neatly with its weaker Situational Judgment score, suggesting that Astra responds differently to explicit playbook instructions than the rest of the field.

5. The multi-expert solution space

We designed Turn 1 as a controlled test to quantify the extent of overlap in attorney judgment while capturing multiple viable approaches to opening negotiation. This multi-expert solution space avoids treating a single attorney's opening move as the only correct answer. We measure the overlap in where attorneys intervene (location consensus) and what actions they choose (action consensus).

5.1 Attorney consensus and variation

Attorneys show substantial overlap in where and how they act.

Table 9. Attorney consensus on location and action, by paragraph and section
MeasureParagraphSection
Locations flagged for action895516
Flagged by four or five attorneys22.3%39.1%
Flagged by two or three34.7%33.5%
Flagged by one attorney42.9%27.3%
Overlap between two attorneys (Jaccard)0.370.52
Share of an attorney's locations a given colleague also flags55.1%70.3%
Disputed: another attorney requires no change14.4%22.7%
Same action where all attorneys act on the same location73.4%63.5%

At the section level, 39.1% of flagged sections are identified by four or five attorneys and 33.5% by two or three, so about 73% are flagged by at least two attorneys. In pairwise comparisons, one attorney flags on average 70.3% of the sections identified by a given colleague.

Action consensus is also substantial. Among attorneys who act at the same location, 73.4% choose the same action at the paragraph level and 63.5% at the section level. Direct disagreement is less common: another attorney requires no change in 14.4% of flagged paragraphs and 22.7% of flagged sections.

We reviewed cases where attorneys chose different actions at the same location. These differences often arose in definitions, miscellaneous provisions, and attached schedules. Some attorneys made direct edits, others used comments, while others left these sections untouched and concentrated their redlines on substantive provisions. These choices therefore represent different viable approaches to the same review. By scoring model redlines against all five attorney rubric sets in Turn 1, we reduce the influence of any individual attorney's preferences while accounting for variation in professional judgment.

Models perform better on judgments shared by more attorneys.

Each column groups a model's Turn 1 Edit, Comment and Escalate rubrics by how many of the scenario's five attorneys flag the paragraph the rubric applies to. Spread: the standard deviation, in points, of the same deliverable's score across the scenario's five rubric sets, averaged.

Model performance rises with attorney consensus. We map each rubric to the paragraph where its required action applies, then group rubric scores by how many attorneys independently target that paragraph. Grok 4.7 scores 67.0% when four or five attorneys flag the paragraph, compared with 39.5% when only one attorney does. Opus 5.5 drops from 65.5% to 30.3%, and Gemini 3.8 Flash from 62.0% to 31.0%. The same pattern holds across the model set: models score substantially higher on the shared core of attorney review than on issues identified by a single attorney. Graded against each of its scenario's five rubric sets, the same model redline varies with a standard deviation of about 13 to 16 points, highlighting the limitation of single-reference evaluation and reinforcing the multi-reference design.
